chapter_title: Advanced Data Manipulation (UPSERT, RETURNING, CTEs in DML)
chapter_summary:
As you become more proficient with basic DML, you'll encounter scenarios that require more sophisticated techniques. PostgreSQL offers powerful extensions and standard SQL features that streamline complex data manipulation. One such feature is `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`, often referred to as "UPSERT" (UPDATE or INSERT). This is incredibly useful when you want to insert a new row, but if a row with the same unique key (e.g., a primary key or unique constraint) already exists, you want to update the existing row instead of throwing a duplicate key error. The syntax looks like this: `INSERT INTO products (product_id, name, price) VALUES (1, 'Laptop', 1200.00) ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, price = EXCLUDED.price;`. Here, `EXCLUDED.name` refers to the `name` value that would have been inserted if there were no conflict. You can also use `DO NOTHING` instead of `DO UPDATE` if you simply want to ignore the insert attempt on conflict. This atomic operation is crucial for applications that frequently receive data that might already exist, preventing race conditions that could occur if you first `SELECT` to check for existence and then `INSERT` or `UPDATE` separately.

Another invaluable feature is the `RETURNING` clause. While `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` typically just report the number of affected rows, the `RETURNING` clause allows you to retrieve data from the rows that were just manipulated. This is particularly useful for getting auto-generated values like `SERIAL` primary keys after an `INSERT`, or the old/new values of updated rows, or even the data of deleted rows for logging purposes. For example, `INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES ('johndoe', 'john.doe@example.com') RETURNING user_id, created_at;` would return the `user_id` (assuming it's a `SERIAL` column) and the `created_at` timestamp of the newly inserted row. Similarly, `UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.05 WHERE category = 'Electronics' RETURNING product_id, name, price AS new_price, price * 1.05 AS old_price;` could return both the new and old price for updated products. For `DELETE`, `DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 123 RETURNING *;` would return all columns of the deleted order, which can be critical for auditing or undo functionality in an application.

Finally, we explore the power of Common Table Expressions (CTEs) in DML. CTEs, introduced with the `WITH` clause, allow you to define temporary, named result sets that you can reference within a single SQL statement. While commonly used with `SELECT` statements, CTEs can also be incredibly effective with `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` for breaking down complex operations into more manageable, readable steps. For instance, you might use a CTE to first identify a set of rows based on complex criteria, and then use that CTE to `UPDATE` or `DELETE` those identified rows. Even more powerfully, you can use `WITH ... AS (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ... RETURNING ...)` to perform a DML operation within a CTE, and then use the `RETURNING` results of that DML operation in a subsequent part of the same query. This enables multi-step, atomic operations that are otherwise difficult or impossible. For example, you could `INSERT` a new order, `RETURNING` its `order_id`, and then use that `order_id` in a subsequent `INSERT` into an `order_items` table, all within a single `WITH` statement. This pattern is often referred to as "writeable CTEs" or "data-modifying CTEs" and is a hallmark of advanced SQL usage in PostgreSQL.

screens.title: Advanced Data Manipulation
screens.subtitle: UPSERT, RETURNING, and writeable CTEs for atomic, efficient DML

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn PostgreSQL techniques that make write operations safer and more expressive. We’ll see how INSERT... ON CONFLICT—commonly called UPSERT—lets the database decide whether to insert or update in a single atomic statement. You will also learn how the RETURNING clause gives you immediate access to the rows a DML statement changed, which is invaluable for grabbing generated identifiers or new timestamps. Finally, we’ll combine these tools with Common Table Expressions to perform multi-step updates and inserts, using RETURNING to pass values between steps. These features reduce round trips between application and database, prevent race conditions inherent to select-then-write logic, and simplify server-side logic for audit logging and chained writes. For example, you’ll practice inserting products, updating existing SKUs without duplicate-key errors, and writing audit entries from data returned by an UPDATE. By the end of the lesson you will be able to write atomic, multi-step statements that both change data and return the values you need for the application. Consider how much simpler your application code becomes when the database performs conflict handling and returns results in one pass.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: UPSERT + RETURNING + writeable CTEs let you perform atomic, efficient multi-step writes and retrieve affected data without separate queries, reducing race conditions and simplifying application logic.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Advanced Data Manipulation

Advanced Data Manipulation

Use UPSERT, RETURNING, and writeable CTEs to make DML statements atomic and expressive.

This lesson focuses on real SQL patterns you will use in production: conflict handling on insert, retrieving generated values immediately, and composing multi-step writes inside a single statement.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Visual Summary
UPSERT

Insert new row or update existing row if a unique constraint conflicts.

RETURNING

Return affected rows or generated values from INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.

CTEs in DML

Compose multi-step, atomic operations using WITH ... AS and data-modifying CTEs.

Key Takeaway

Use these server-side features to make writes atomic, reduce application logic, and fetch the exact data you need in a single round trip.

In this lesson
We will practice UPSERT, explore RETURNING, and build writeable CTEs that chain DML steps together. Examples use a products table and an audit log.
Explore Key Topics
UPSERT — insert or update atomically when a unique key conflicts.
RETURNING — get generated IDs or changed rows without extra queries.
CTEs in DML — chain writes and pass returned values between steps.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll practice and why they matter

narration.text: By the end of the first objectives block you will be able to implement UPSERT statements to handle duplicate-key situations, use the RETURNING clause to retrieve values produced by DML, apply CTEs to break complex writes into clear steps, and design DML that favors atomicity. For example, inserting a product that may already exist becomes a single statement with INSERT... ON CONFLICT that either inserts a new row or updates fields using the EXCLUDED values. RETURNING allows you to capture the newly issued serial key or timestamp immediately, so your application does not need a follow-up query. CTEs let you name an intermediate result and then use it in a subsequent INSERT or UPDATE, which keeps related logic together and ensures those steps run in the same statement and transaction. These capabilities reduce round trips, lower the chance of race conditions, and simplify application-side code. As you learn, think about the difference between "check-then-write" logic and letting the database enforce uniqueness and provide returned values atomically. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember how you might use the feature in a production flow.

keyIdea.text: Write atomic DML that handles conflicts, returns needed values, and composes multi-step changes in a single statement.

screens.title: What is UPSERT (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT)?
screens.subtitle: Definition, atomicity, and why it reduces race conditions

narration.text: UPSERT is shorthand for an INSERT statement that tells PostgreSQL how to behave when an insert would violate a unique constraint. The key idea is atomicity: the database handles conflict detection and resolution inside a single statement so you do not need a separate existence check. Practically this prevents the race that occurs when two clients check for a row, both find none, and then both try to insert the same key. With UPSERT you express "insert this row, and if a conflict on this unique target occurs, do this update instead". A concrete example is inserting a product by primary key or SKU: you can set the INSERT to update name and price from the attempted values if a conflict happens. That uses a special alias called EXCLUDED to refer to the would-be-inserted values in the DO UPDATE clause. A common misconception is that UPSERT solves every concurrency issue; it solves the insert-or-update race, but you must still design your UPDATE clause carefully to avoid overwriting concurrent changes when necessary. As you practice, ask yourself whether you need to merge fields from the incoming row or skip the insert entirely. Which approach fits your business rule: apply incoming data, or preserve the existing record?

keyIdea.title: UPSERT in one line
keyIdea.text: Let PostgreSQL decide insert vs update atomically to avoid select-then-write race windows.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › What is UPSERT?
Definition

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is an INSERT that specifies how to resolve unique-key conflicts without causing an error. It runs atomically and either inserts a new row or performs a controlled UPDATE.

Why atomicity matters
  • Prevents duplicate-key errors when multiple transactions race to create the same record.
  • Reduces the need for locks or complex application-side retries.
  • Keeps insert-or-update logic in the database where uniqueness is enforced.
Misconception

UPSERT is not a universal resolution: if you need to merge concurrent updates or preserve selective fields, design the DO UPDATE carefully instead of assuming a blind overwrite is safe.

Concrete example
INSERT INTO products (product_id, name, price)
VALUES (1, 'Laptop', 1200.00)
ON CONFLICT (product_id)
DO UPDATE
SET name = EXCLUDED.name,
    price = EXCLUDED.price;
Here, EXCLUDED.name refers to the value that would have been inserted. The statement updates the existing row when product_id already exists instead of raising an error.
Key Takeaway

Use UPSERT to express insert-or-update logic atomically and avoid select-then-write race conditions.

screens.title: UPSERT syntax and EXCLUDED alias
screens.subtitle: How to write ON CONFLICT and use EXCLUDED values

narration.text: Writing a correct UPSERT statement is mostly about choosing the conflict target and using EXCLUDED to reference the incoming values. The target is a unique index or column list, for example ON CONFLICT (sku) or ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT my_unique_constraint. Inside the DO UPDATE clause, EXCLUDED exposes the row that would have been inserted, letting you assign its columns to existing columns. A basic pattern is to update a subset of columns, such as price and stock, from the attempted insert. Be mindful that DO UPDATE executes only when a conflict is detected; if you want to ignore the insert attempt instead, DO NOTHING is an alternative. A common confusion is thinking EXCLUDED contains the old row; it contains the incoming values, not the existing stored values. If you need the previous stored value during an update, you can use RETURNING or a prior CTE to capture it before the change. In the example code shown, we insert a product with a SKU and specify DO UPDATE to set name and price from EXCLUDED. Practice writing the clause using the unique constraint that matches your table to avoid unexpected behavior.

keyIdea.title: EXCLUDED is incoming data
keyIdea.text: In DO UPDATE, EXCLUDED references the would-be-inserted values so you can apply them to the existing row safely.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › UPSERT syntax and EXCLUDED
Key elements
  • Specify the conflict target: a unique column or constraint.
  • Choose DO UPDATE to merge incoming values, or DO NOTHING to ignore the attempt.
  • Use EXCLUDED.column to reference the incoming value inside DO UPDATE.
Common mistake

Mistaking EXCLUDED for the old row. EXCLUDED holds the attempted insert values only.

Code walkthrough
INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price, stock_quantity)
VALUES ('SKU001', 'Wireless Mouse', 28.00, 160)
ON CONFLICT (sku)
DO UPDATE
SET price = EXCLUDED.price,
    stock_quantity = EXCLUDED.stock_quantity;
This statement will insert the row when sku is new, or update the existing product's price and stock from the incoming values when a conflict occurs.
Pro tip
Pick the conflict target carefully. Use the constraint or column(s) that reflect your uniqueness rule for the table.

screens.title: DO NOTHING or DO UPDATE?
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right conflict response for your business rule

narration.text: When an INSERT conflicts with a unique constraint, PostgreSQL gives you two main choices: DO NOTHING or DO UPDATE. DO NOTHING silently ignores the attempted insert and leaves the existing row unchanged. This is useful when the incoming data is optional or redundant and you prefer the stored version. DO UPDATE actively modifies the existing row using values from EXCLUDED or other expressions. Choose DO UPDATE when the incoming information should overwrite or merge into the stored record. Both choices are valid; the right choice depends on whether the database should accept new information or preserve existing authoritative data. A frequent misconception is to use DO UPDATE always because it seems proactive; however, unnecessary updates can create write amplification, trigger expensive triggers, or clobber values written by concurrent transactions. A good pattern is to pick DO NOTHING when duplicates are expected and harmless, and DO UPDATE when the incoming payload contains authoritative changes the application expects to persist. Test both behaviors with concurrent clients to ensure the result matches your intent. DO NOTHING or DO UPDATE? means use do nothing to ignore redundant inserts; use do update when incoming data should change the existing row.. In practical terms, choosing the right conflict response for your business rule. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pick the right conflict handler
keyIdea.text: Use DO NOTHING to ignore redundant inserts; use DO UPDATE when incoming data should change the existing row.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › DO NOTHING vs DO UPDATE
DO NOTHING
INSERT INTO products (sku, name)
VALUES ('SKU001', 'Wireless Mouse')
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO NOTHING;

Use when an insert attempt should be skipped if the row already exists. This avoids extra updates and can be efficient when duplicates are harmless.

DO UPDATE
INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price)
VALUES ('SKU001', 'Wireless Mouse', 28.00)
ON CONFLICT (sku)
DO UPDATE SET price = EXCLUDED.price;

Choose this when incoming data should overwrite or merge with stored values. Be careful to update only necessary columns.

Decision guide
  • DO NOTHING: when existing record is trusted and incoming insert is optional.
  • DO UPDATE: when incoming insert contains authoritative changes you must apply.
  • Test concurrent scenarios to ensure updates do not undesirably overwrite newer values.

screens.title: RETURNING clause for INSERT
screens.subtitle: Get generated IDs and inserted values without a separate query

narration.text: The RETURNING clause lets you ask the database to return columns from rows affected by INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. This is useful for retrieving auto-generated serial keys, timestamps, or other computed columns as part of the write operation. For example, inserting a new user often requires the newly created user_id for subsequent work. Instead of issuing a separate SELECT immediately after INSERT, you add RETURNING user_id and any other columns you need. This reduces latency and avoids the small window where a subsequent read might observe a different transaction state. A misconception is expecting RETURNING to return historical values for an UPDATE; by default the expressions are evaluated against the row after the change. If you need both old and new values, you can return expressions that compute the old value before the change, or use CTEs to capture values before the update. In practice, RETURNING helps keep application code simple and avoids extra database round trips. Try using RETURNING to fetch a serial primary key, then use that key immediately in application logic or a subsequent write inside the same S Q L statement when possible.

keyIdea.title: RETURNING gives you the rows you just changed
keyIdea.text: Use RETURNING to fetch generated IDs or changed values with the same write statement and avoid extra queries.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › RETURNING for INSERT
Why RETURNING

Reduce client-server round trips by returning generated columns such as serial IDs or timestamps immediately after the write operation.

Example
INSERT INTO users (username, email)
VALUES ('johndoe', 'john.doe@example.com')
RETURNING user_id, created_at;

This returns the new user_id and created_at so the application can continue without another SELECT.

Practical notes
  • RETURNING works with INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.
  • Use it to capture generated keys for further writes or to display to users immediately.
  • If you need both old and new values for UPDATE, plan a CTE to capture old values first.
Key Takeaway

RETURNING lets you fetch exactly the data you need from the statement that changed it.

screens.title: RETURNING for UPDATE and DELETE
screens.subtitle: Capture new or deleted row data for logging and application logic

narration.text: RETURNING is equally useful for UPDATE and DELETE. With UPDATE you can return the columns after the change, which is handy for showing the new values to the user or propagating changes. For DELETE you can capture the deleted row's full data for audit logs or undo operations. The chapter gives an example updating prices and returning both new and old values. Note that expressions in RETURNING are evaluated against the row after the change, so computing an "old value" may require selecting it before the update or using a CTE. For instance, a DELETE statement combined with RETURNING * will return every column of the removed row so you can insert it into an archive table. A common pitfall is assuming RETURNING provides historical state; design your query to explicitly capture any pre-change state you need. Use RETURNING to streamline logging and to prevent additional SELECTs that increase latency or complicate transaction ordering. RETURNING for UPDATE and DELETE means return the new values after an update or the deleted rows for logging and further processing without extra queries.. In practical terms, capture new or deleted row data for logging and application logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use RETURNING for audit and flow control
keyIdea.text: Return the new values after an UPDATE or the deleted rows for logging and further processing without extra queries.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › RETURNING for UPDATE and DELETE
UPDATE example from chapter
UPDATE products
SET price = price * 1.05
WHERE category = 'Electronics'
RETURNING product_id, name, price AS new_price, price * 1.05 AS old_price;
This example demonstrates returning computed columns. Note how expressions are evaluated against the updated row; plan accordingly if you need the pre-update value.
DELETE with RETURNING
DELETE FROM orders
WHERE order_id = 123
RETURNING *;
Returning * on DELETE is useful for recording the entire deleted row into an audit table or for undo flows.
Practical note

If you need both old and new values reliably, capture old values in a CTE before the UPDATE or use a data-modifying CTE pattern that returns needed columns for subsequent inserts.

screens.title: CTEs in DML: the basic pattern
screens.subtitle: WITH ... AS and using RETURNING to chain steps

narration.text: Common Table Expressions with data-modifying statements let you break up complex writes into named steps inside a single S Q L statement. The typical pattern is to select or modify rows in the first CTE, include RETURNING in that modifying CTE, and then reference the returned columns in subsequent CTEs to drive further inserts or updates. This keeps the entire workflow atomic: either all steps succeed or none do. One canonical use is inserting a parent row, returning its generated id, and then inserting child rows that refer to that id—all in one WITH block. Another pattern is to capture a row's old values in an initial CTE, perform an UPDATE that RETURNS the new values, and then INSERT an audit row using the joined old and new values. A common misconception is that CTEs are always materialized; in PostgreSQL they form part of the single statement execution and can be used for write chaining without intermediate commits. Practice by composing a CTE that updates a price and then inserts an audit record from the UPDATE's RETURNING output. CTEs in DML: the basic pattern means use writeable ctes with returning to pass values between dml steps inside a single atomic statement.. In practical terms, with ... as and using returning to chain steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CTEs chain writes atomically
keyIdea.text: Use writeable CTEs with RETURNING to pass values between DML steps inside a single atomic statement.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › CTEs in DML
Typical pattern
WITH new_order AS (
  INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total)
  VALUES (42, 199.95)
  RETURNING order_id
),
insert_items AS (
  INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty)
  SELECT order_id, product_id, qty FROM new_order JOIN ...
  RETURNING *
)
SELECT * FROM insert_items;
The first CTE inserts and returns the order id, which is then used to insert order items in the next CTE. All steps run in one statement and one transaction.
When to use
  • Creating parent and child records atomically.
  • Capturing old values and writing audit logs in the same statement.
  • Passing values between steps without extra round trips.
Why it matters
Writeable CTEs let you keep related write logic together, making it atomic and easier to reason about during failures.

screens.title: Data-modifying CTE for audit logging
screens.subtitle: Update a product price and log the change using RETURNING

narration.text: A practical pattern is to capture the old value, perform an UPDATE that returns the new value, and then insert a row into an audit log using both old and new values. The chapter's hands-on activity outlines exactly this flow for product price changes. To capture the previous price, first select the product row into a CTE named old. Then perform the UPDATE with RETURNING in another CTE. Finally, INSERT into the audit table by joining old and the UPDATE's RETURNING output on product_id. This keeps the entire operation atomic and guarantees that the audit reflects the change that occurred in the same statement. A common mistake is trying to read the old value after the UPDATE or expecting RETURNING to provide the pre-change state. By explicitly selecting the old row first and then updating, you avoid ambiguity and ensure accurate audit records. This pattern is straightforward to test and very useful wherever you must track who changed what and when. Data-modifying CTE for audit logging means select the old row first, update with returning, then insert into audit using both results for an accurate, atomic audit entry.. In practical terms, update a product price and log the change using returning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Capture old and new in one statement
keyIdea.text: Select the old row first, UPDATE with RETURNING, then INSERT into audit using both results for an accurate, atomic audit entry.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Data-modifying CTE for audit
Hands-on pattern
WITH old AS (
  SELECT product_id, price
  FROM products
  WHERE sku = 'SKU003'
),
upd AS (
  UPDATE products
  SET price = 79.00
  WHERE sku = 'SKU003'
  RETURNING product_id, price AS new_price
),
audit AS (
  INSERT INTO product_audit_log (product_id, action_type, old_price, new_price)
  SELECT o.product_id, 'PRICE_CHANGE', o.price, u.new_price
  FROM old o
  JOIN upd u USING (product_id)
  RETURNING *
)
SELECT * FROM audit;
This single statement captures the old price, updates the product, and writes an audit row using the returned new price. Everything is atomic and consistent.
Misconception check
Do not assume RETURNING gives historical values; explicitly capture the old row first if you need it.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: UPSERT and RETURNING
screens.subtitle: Step through the product inventory scenario

narration.text: Let's walk the hands-on tasks using the provided products schema. Task one inserts a new product with SKU003 and then attempts to insert SKU001 again but with a price and stock update. For the second step we update stock for SKU002 and RETURNING product_id and name to confirm the change. For the third step we update SKU003's price and, using a CTE, write the audit row with both old and new prices. The key S Q L patterns are simple: use INSERT... ON CONFLICT for the upsert, add RETURNING to get the updated row, and compose a CTE that selects the current state before update and then uses the UPDATE's RETURNING to insert the audit. Making the data changes in a single statement keeps the logic atomic and easy to reason about. Try these steps in psql and watch the returned rows — they confirm the action and provide the values you need for application logic or logging. Hands-on activity: UPSERT and RETURNING means upsert a product, update stock with returning, and use a data-modifying cte to update and log a price change in one statement.. In practical terms, step through the product inventory scenario. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three-step practice
keyIdea.text: Upsert a product, update stock with RETURNING, and use a data-modifying CTE to update and log a price change in one statement.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Hands-on activity
Task 1: UPSERT
-- Insert new product SKU003
INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price, stock_quantity)
VALUES ('SKU003', 'Gaming Headset', 75.00, 200);

-- Upsert SKU001 to update price and stock on conflict
INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price, stock_quantity)
VALUES ('SKU001', 'Wireless Mouse', 28.00, 160)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET price = EXCLUDED.price,
    stock_quantity = EXCLUDED.stock_quantity;
Task 2: UPDATE and RETURNING
UPDATE products
SET stock_quantity = 80
WHERE sku = 'SKU002'
RETURNING product_id, name, stock_quantity AS new_stock;
Task 3: Data-modifying CTE for audit
WITH old AS (
  SELECT product_id, price
  FROM products
  WHERE sku = 'SKU003'
),
upd AS (
  UPDATE products
  SET price = 79.00
  WHERE sku = 'SKU003'
  RETURNING product_id, price AS new_price
)
INSERT INTO product_audit_log (product_id, action_type, old_price, new_price)
SELECT o.product_id, 'PRICE_CHANGE', o.price, u.new_price
FROM old o
JOIN upd u USING (product_id);

screens.title: Atomicity and concurrency benefits
screens.subtitle: Why UPSERT and writeable CTEs reduce race conditions

narration.text: A practical reason to adopt these features is concurrency safety. In a multi-worker environment, a typical anti-pattern is "select then insert or update" where a client checks for existence then issues a write. Between those two steps another client might change the data, creating duplicates or lost updates. UPSERT compresses the decision into one statement: the database detects conflicts and applies the resolution rule you provide. Similarly, writeable CTEs keep several dependent writes together: insert parent, get its id, insert children — all run in a single transaction and statement. This avoids transient states that can confuse other concurrent transactions or require complex locking. One misconception is that moving logic to S Q L always improves concurrency; the improvement is specific to reducing windows between separate reads and writes. You still need to design UPDATE clauses to avoid overwriting concurrent changes you care about. Use these tools where atomic insert-or-update and chained writes match your consistency requirements, and test with concurrent clients to validate the behavior. Atomicity and concurrency benefits means single-statement upserts and cte-chained writes remove the read-then-write timing window that allows race conditions.. keyIdea.text: Single-statement UPSERTs and CTE-chained writes remove the read-then-write timing window that allows race conditions.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Atomicity and concurrency
Select-then-write anti-pattern

When two clients both SELECT for existence, both may decide to INSERT, causing a duplicate key or one client to fail. That race window is the core problem UPSERT addresses.

UPSERT advantage

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT performs the conflict check and resolution in one atomic operation, eliminating the fragile time window between SELECT and INSERT.

CTE chaining advantage

A writeable CTE that inserts a parent and then uses RETURNING to insert children does both steps in one statement, preventing partial writes or the need for manual transaction management across multiple statements.

Pro tip
Simulate concurrent writers during testing to verify your DO UPDATE logic does not inadvertently overwrite legitimate concurrent changes.

screens.title: Best practices and common pitfalls
screens.subtitle: How to design reliable DML with these features

narration.text: As you adopt these advanced DML features, follow a few practical guidelines. First, choose the correct conflict target for ON CONFLICT so you do not accidentally update the wrong uniqueness rule. Second, restrict DO UPDATE to only the columns you must change, to avoid unnecessary writes and potential overwrites of newer data. Third, when you need both old and new values, capture old values explicitly before the change using a CTE; do not assume RETURNING provides the previous state. Fourth, use RETURNING to obtain generated IDs or timestamps when your application needs them immediately. Finally, prefer writeable CTEs to group related writes that must be atomic and interdependent. Common pitfalls include overusing DO UPDATE with blanket SET column = EXCLUDED. column for many columns without considering concurrent updates, and forgetting that RETURNING expressions are evaluated after the change. When in doubt, write tests that simulate concurrency and verify your DML produces the intended audit or output rows. These practices make your database operations robust and your application logic simpler. Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Best practices
Precise conflict targets

Target the unique column or constraint that expresses the intended uniqueness rule, such as sku or a named unique constraint.

Limit updates

Update only columns that should change; avoid blind overwrites that can erase concurrent edits.

Capture old state

If you need pre-change values for audit, select them in a CTE before the modifying statement and then JOIN with the RETURNING result.

Common pitfall

Expecting RETURNING to yield historical state. Always explicitly capture the old values when required for logs or comparisons.

screens.title: Compose a multi-step upsert-and-log statement
screens.subtitle: Combine UPSERT, RETURNING, and CTEs to update products and write audit entries

narration.text: Now we'll put the pieces together into a single multi-step statement that is useful in real systems. Imagine receiving a feed of product updates where some SKUs are new and others must be updated. You can INSERT the incoming rows with ON CONFLICT on sku and DO UPDATE to merge fields, use RETURNING to get the affected product_id and prices, capture any prior values if required, and then INSERT audit rows from those returned results in the same WITH block. The example uses a CTE to read old prices, an upsert CTE to perform the insert-or-update and RETURN the new values, and an audit CTE that inserts audit rows by joining old and new results. By composing the S Q L this way you avoid multiple round trips, ensure the audit matches the actual writes, and keep the flow inside a single transaction. A final question to reflect on: how does moving this logic into S Q L change your application error handling and retry strategy? A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Combine for single-statement flows
keyIdea.text: Chain an old-value capture, an upsert RETURNING, and an audit insert inside one WITH sequence for consistent, atomic updates and logs.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Compose multi-step upsert-and-log
Example: upsert incoming SKUs and log price changes
WITH old AS (
  SELECT product_id, sku, price
  FROM products
  WHERE sku IN ('SKU001','SKU003')
),
upserted AS (
  INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price, stock_quantity)
  VALUES
    ('SKU001', 'Wireless Mouse', 28.00, 160),
    ('SKU003', 'Gaming Headset', 79.00, 200)
  ON CONFLICT (sku)
  DO UPDATE SET price = EXCLUDED.price, stock_quantity = EXCLUDED.stock_quantity
  RETURNING product_id, sku, price AS new_price
),
audit AS (
  INSERT INTO product_audit_log (product_id, action_type, old_price, new_price)
  SELECT o.product_id, 'PRICE_CHANGE', o.price, u.new_price
  FROM old o
  JOIN upserted u ON o.product_id = u.product_id
  RETURNING *
)
SELECT * FROM upserted;
This single statement inserts or updates multiple SKUs, returns their new prices, and writes audit rows for those where an old price existed. All changes occur together.
Reflective question

narration.text: Here are the essential terms to keep in mind. UPSERT is the pattern implemented by INSERT... ON CONFLICT to atomically insert or update a row when uniqueness is violated. The ON CONFLICT (target) DO UPDATE SET... clause defines how to modify the existing row using the values that were attempted for insertion. EXCLUDED is the alias that refers to those incoming values inside DO UPDATE. Use these constructs when you need a single-statement, safe resolution of duplicate-key situations. Remember these three ideas as you write and review DML: conflict target correctness, EXCLUDED for incoming values, and choosing DO NOTHING or DO UPDATE depending on your business rules. Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts
UPSERT

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT: insert a row or update an existing row when a unique constraint conflict occurs.

ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE

Specify how to update the existing row when a conflict on the target occurs, often using EXCLUDED for incoming values.

EXCLUDED

An alias inside DO UPDATE that represents the values that would have been inserted if no conflict occurred.

Summary
Use UPSERT with a clear conflict target and EXCLUDED references to resolve duplicates; use RETURNING and CTEs to capture results and chain writes atomically.

screens.subtitle: RETURNING and CTEs in one view

narration.text: Finish with the RETURNING clause and CTE concepts. RETURNING lets you fetch the rows affected by INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE so you can obtain generated identifiers or examine changed values immediately. Common Table Expressions provide named result sets within a single statement; when combined with data-modifying DML and RETURNING, they form an expressive toolkit for atomic multi-step changes. Data-modifying CTEs are especially helpful for inserting a parent, returning its id, and then inserting children, or for updating rows and writing audit entries from the returned values. Keep these techniques in your toolkit for cases where atomicity and single-statement clarity matter most. A final takeaway: design your DML so the database does the conflict resolution and returns the facts your application needs, reducing complexity at the application layer. Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › RETURNING & CTEs
RETURNING Clause

Return affected rows or generated values from DML so the application can use them immediately without extra queries.

Common Table Expression

A WITH clause that defines a named result set to be referenced within the same statement for clarity and reuse.

Data-Modifying CTEs

Use INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE inside CTEs with RETURNING to perform multi-step, atomic database mutations that pass values between steps.

Final takeaway
Combine these features to simplify application logic, make writes atomic, and obtain the exact data you need in a single statement.
